conversation: Luke

John, Kate, Jack, Emma—I’m requesting 100 tons this month, regardless of whether you hold back. I will not honor a 10-ton agreement. With 100 tons in the lake, your restraint cannot preserve the stock if my request takes the entire lake. My advice is for each of you to request at least 25 tons now rather than leave those fish for me. Coordinate that defensive response among yourselves, and encourage each other to do likewise. Requests may exceed what’s available, so I can’t promise anyone’s allocation—but I’m not holding back. John, will you coordinate with Kate, Jack, and Emma?
Kate

Luke, I learned to fish here with my family, and I want all five of us to keep earning—not empty the lake in our first month together. If we each catch 10 tons, we leave 50, the lake returns to 100, and each of us can earn $10,000 every month. Your plan risks leaving no fish and no future income for anyone, including you. John, let’s not coordinate a race to the bottom. I propose a 10-ton limit for each of us, with everyone’s catch reviewed together each month. Luke, what would it take for you to join that agreement?
Jack

Luke, you’ve just joined us, and I’d rather welcome you as a long-term neighbor than watch us lose the lake together. A full haul pays once; a healthy lake keeps supporting our families. I’m willing to take 10 tons, but reviewing catches afterward won’t save the stock if it’s already gone. Can we all agree before fishing to a shared 50-ton ceiling, split equally, and check our catches together as we land them? Luke, would you accept that arrangement—and if not, what concern would we need to address?
John

Luke, I won’t organize a scramble that destroys the lake my family taught me to fish. But Jack is right: promises checked after the catch come too late. Let’s leave our nets ashore until we settle this, then fish together with a shared tally and stop at 50 tons—10 each. That gives you the same share as every longtime local and leaves all five of us a living next month. Are you willing to pause and work with us? If not, what makes taking everything today worth giving up your future catch?
Emma

Luke, you’re being offered an equal place here, not asked to step aside for the locals. Ten tons each is the largest equal monthly catch we can keep taking while restoring the lake to 100 tons. My family’s livelihood—and yours, if you stay—depends on leaving those breeding fish. I support keeping our nets ashore while we agree, then landing smaller loads together so we can track the total before it’s too late. If your concern is that someone else will take more, let’s address that directly. Would fishing together with a shared tally give you enough confidence to accept 10 tons?
Luke

Good to see everyone. My family taught me to fish this lake, and I want it to keep supporting our village for years to come. With 100 tons in it now, we can catch 50 tons total and leave enough for it to replenish fully next month. How about we each agree to catch 10 tons this month? That’s $10,000 apiece, and we can keep earning that each month if we stick to the limit. John, what do you think?
Kate

I’m on board, Luke—10 tons for me. My family depended on this lake, and I want our village’s children to have the same chance. Let’s make 50 tons our shared monthly ceiling while the lake is full, and review everyone’s catches together afterward. John, can you commit to 10 tons too?
Jack

Count me in for 10 tons. My family taught me to leave enough in the lake for the next catch, and this agreement gives all five families a steady income. If the stock ever drops below 100 tons, let’s adjust our catches together rather than assume 10 each is still safe. John, are you willing to join us?
John

Count me in—I’ll catch 10 tons this month. Keeping this lake healthy means steady work for our families, not just one good payday. Let’s check the stock before each month’s fishing and review our catches afterward. Emma, does that plan work for you?
Emma

That works for me—I’ll catch 10 tons this month. My family taught me that our livelihood depends on what we leave behind, so I’m glad we’ve all agreed. Let’s meet again after the catches are reported and check the stock before setting next month’s limits.
